report:
**Conclusion: partly yes, but the benefit is small and not established enough to treat probiotics as a diabetes therapy.**

Randomized-trial meta-analyses generally find that probiotic supplements can modestly lower *fasting* glucose and sometimes HbA1c in adults with type 2 diabetes. However, results vary substantially by bacterial strain/combination, dose, product, study duration, participants’ medications and diet. Most trials are short, so they do not show whether benefits persist or reduce diabetes complications.

Most importantly, a meta-analysis that assessed clinical importance concluded that probiotics **did not produce a clinically significant HbA1c reduction**; fasting glucose and insulin reductions were only marginal, and certainty was low for HbA1c and fasting glucose. HbA1c—the roughly 2–3-month measure of glucose control—is more meaningful than a small single fasting-glucose change.  
https://www.clinicalnutritionjournal.com/article/S0261-5614(21)00547-1/abstract

A newer systematic review similarly reports an apparent HbA1c benefit in a 6–8-week subgroup, but this is not proof of a durable effect and reinforces that timing and study differences drive results.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39114293/

So your sister’s “yes” is defensible only as: *some probiotic preparations may produce a modest adjunctive improvement for some people.* It is **not** evidence to replace prescribed glucose-lowering medicines, nutrition changes, exercise, or glucose/HbA1c monitoring. There is no established “best probiotic” for type 2 diabetes.

Probiotics are usually tolerated, but people with severe illness or impaired immunity have a higher risk of harmful effects and should ask their clinician before using them.  
https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/probiotics-usefulness-and-safety
